security_audit.summary: Most Ruby backtick detections are false positives caused by Markdown code fences in this design guide. The audit confirmed real instructional risks around shell execution, file writes, environment forwarding, arbitrary URL fetches, screenshots, raw context injection, and generated MCP tools. No prompt-injection attempt against the audit instructions was found in the skill text.

remediation.suggestion: Replace shell=True and subprocess.getoutput examples with argument arrays, shell=False, strict command allowlists, and quoting for paths.
Normalize paths, require workspace containment, reject traversal, and ask for approval before writes or generated-code persistence.
Add URL allowlists, timeouts, size limits, content-type checks, and prompt boundaries for untrusted web or file content.
Require explicit user consent before screenshots, redact secrets, limit page scope, and disable automatic image sharing by default.
Require human review, static scanning, sandboxed installation, and signed approval before connecting generated MCP server code.

semantic_findings.title: Prompt Injection Exposure in Raw Context Assembly
semantic_findings.description: The context manager fetches URL content and inserts file or URL content directly into prompts without separating untrusted instructions from trusted control text.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The cited code directly combines external web content and file content into the model prompt. That is a clear prompt-injection exposure for autonomous agents.

semantic_findings.title: Shell Injection in Checkpoint Workspace Capture
semantic_findings.description: The checkpoint manager interpolates the workspace path into shell commands passed to subprocess.getoutput, which can execute unintended shell syntax if the path is hostile.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The workspace value is formatted directly into shell command strings. There is no quoting, argument array, or validation at the call site.

semantic_findings.title: Unvalidated LLM-Generated MCP Tool Creation
semantic_findings.description: The MCP pattern generates server code from a user description, writes it to disk, and connects it without human review, static scanning, sandboxing, or signing.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The data flow from user description to generated code to connected server is explicit. The example does not show any validation gate before loading the tool.

semantic_findings.title: Screenshot Data Sent to Vision Model
semantic_findings.description: The browser and visual agent examples capture screenshots and include image data in model requests or metadata, which can disclose sensitive page content.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The examples explicitly capture screenshots and pass them into model-facing structures. Sensitive browser state can be present in those images.

content.value_statement: Autonomous coding agents need reliable tool design, permission gates, and context control. This skill provides practical patterns for agent loops, tool schemas, browser actions, and human approvals.
actual_capabilities: Explains think, decide, act, and observe loops for autonomous agents.
Defines tool schema patterns for file, terminal, browser, and context tools.
Describes permission levels and approval flows for risky actions.
Shows sandboxing concepts for command allowlists and workspace isolation.
Covers browser automation and visual page interaction patterns.
Outlines context management, checkpoints, and MCP tool creation patterns.
limitations: Provides design patterns and examples, not a complete agent framework.
Code samples require security hardening before production use.
Does not include runnable tests or packaged libraries.
Focuses on Python-style examples that may need adaptation.

use_cases.title: Design a Coding Agent Architecture
use_cases.description: Plan an agent loop, tool registry, model routing, and result handling before implementation.

use_cases.title: Add Permission Controls
use_cases.description: Map tool actions to approval levels, block dangerous operations, and define safer execution rules.

use_cases.title: Prototype Browser and MCP Tools
use_cases.description: Sketch browser automation, visual interaction, context capture, checkpointing, and MCP integration flows.

prompt_templates.title: Map a Basic Agent Loop
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner planning for a new agent.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the autonomous-agent-patterns skill to outline a basic coding agent loop for my project. Include tools, observations, stopping rules, and user approval points.

prompt_templates.title: Design Tool Schemas
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the skill to design tool schemas for file reading, file editing, terminal commands, and browser actions. Include required arguments and expected results.

prompt_templates.title: Review Permission Levels
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the skill to review my planned agent tools. Classify each tool as automatic, ask once, ask every time, or never allowed, and explain each choice.

prompt_templates.title: Harden an Agent Workflow
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the skill to harden an autonomous coding agent design. Focus on sandboxing, prompt injection, screenshot privacy, checkpoint safety, MCP loading, and audit logging.

output_examples.input: I need a permission model for a coding agent that can edit files and run tests.
output: A permission matrix that separates read-only tools from write and command tools.
Approval guidance for file edits, test runs, package installs, and destructive commands.
Safety notes for workspace boundaries, audit logs, and rollback steps.

output_examples.input: I want an agent to inspect a web page and click the right control.
output: A browser automation flow with navigation, page state capture, element selection, and post-action observation.
Privacy warnings for screenshots and guidance to redact sensitive page content before model analysis.

output_examples.input: I need checkpoint and resume behavior for long-running agent tasks.
output: A checkpoint plan that records history, context, workspace state, and metadata.
Recovery guidance for restoring state while validating paths and avoiding unsafe shell calls.

best_practices: Treat every tool call as a permissioned action with clear risk labels.
Keep browser screenshots and external content isolated from trusted instructions.
Add audit logs and rollback steps for file and command changes.
anti_patterns: Running shell commands from model text without approval or argument lists.
Writing generated tool code directly into a live server.
Mixing untrusted file or web content with system instructions in one prompt.

faq.question: What does this skill help me build?
faq.answer: It helps design autonomous coding agents with tool use, permissions, browser automation, context handling, and checkpoints.

faq.question: Is this a runnable framework?
faq.answer: No. It is a design guide with example patterns that need implementation and testing.

faq.question: Does it cover security controls?
faq.answer: Yes. It discusses permission levels, approval flows, command sandboxing, and dangerous operation handling.

faq.question: Can I use it with Claude Code or Codex?
faq.answer: Yes. The patterns apply to Claude, Codex, Claude Code, and similar tool-using coding agents.

faq.question: What should I review before production use?
faq.answer: Review shell execution, file writes, network fetches, screenshots, prompt injection boundaries, and generated MCP code.

faq.question: Does it include MCP integration ideas?
faq.answer: Yes. It outlines dynamic MCP server discovery and generated tool creation patterns.
